segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Record and post everywhere!

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Perfect.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And please do with public domain!

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: OK, great. Well, that makes it easy because I know Caitlin reviewed the form, but the the three check marks on the form were mostly just making sure you're comfortable with recording the interview, transcribing the interview, and then having any quotations in your interview being ascribed by name to you.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Would love it, post it – public domain.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Perfect, wonderful. Yeah, and hopefully we could put on the Internet archive, so that would be great.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Well, I thought I thought we just jump in because hopefully we can cover a fair bit of ground today.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: So Brewster, I thought we might start if we could go way back in time to your time at MIT and, you know, where the origin of your idea of creating a new "Library of Alexandria" came from?
segments.clip_title: The Question That Started It All

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Actually, it was a friend of mine [who] challenged me.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: He said "Brewster, you're an idealist." I said, "yes and a technologist, yes." And he said, "paint a portrait that is better because of the future. That's better because of your technology." And this turned out to be extremely hard! So I walked back and forth over the bridge, back and forth from Boston to Cambridge as I walked back and forth to school. And I could only come up with two ideas. And one was too obvious. So I thought other people would do it. So I went for the other one, which was to try to protect people's privacy because people are just going to throw it away. And this is 1980. And so I went off to try to figure out how to make computer chips to go and encrypt people's phone conversations, and I figured that I had to make it so cheap and offer other features other than privacy, because nobody's going to pay for privacy and they're not going to do anything for privacy, they're just going to throw it away. But I found that I couldn't. So after a while of building chips and things, I couldn't figure out how to do it cheaply enough. So I went to Plan B, which was to build the Library of Alexandria version two. How do you make all the published works of humankind available to everybody, forever, for free?
segments.clip_title: Plan B: The Library of Alexandria, Version Two

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And can you make it so that if you... Any one who was curious enough to want to have access to to these materials, that they could get access. That seemed like a good technical problem to work on.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah, which is an ambitious Plan B! And so I know around this time that you, you start working with Danny Hillis and then Thinking Machines. And one thing before I ask you about that, I'm curious... And I'm curious what your thoughts on this is that you and Danny Hillis are working at Thinking Machines. And then later, Hillis ends up as part of the Long Now Foundation. You're working on the Internet Archive. You know, it just seems like sort of complimentary aims, and I'm just curious...

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Yeah, well, then Danny is one of my two mentors. There's Danny Hillis and Bill Dunn. Bill Dunn is interesting. He invented the term metadata, you know, anyway. Yeah. He said the metadata is more important than the data itself. This was the mid-80s. This is like this guy is way, way ahead! Completely awesome. But Danny. Yeah, I learned so much from Danny and I worked I just tried to make Danny's ideas go real. So, yeah, he helped me every step of the way.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: And had you been exposed to any history at MIT? Like, did this interest come from a technology background or was there a...

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: I think its technology, really. In that it's... If you're going to build a new publishing system, we knew back in 1980, I mean, remember that this is, you know, there wasn't a Macintosh yet. There was an Apple 2, right, there? The IBM PC was new then. Right. You know, there's there was the ARPANET, [which] was basically, you know, barely working. There were still mainframes, basically did accounting and, you know, trajectories of missiles and crap. But we knew a new generation of publishing was coming up, of how people communicated with each other. There's the Memex, you know, a vision by Vannevar Bush. There is Ted Nelson's Xanadu, and hypertext systems. There is, you know, screens, you know, we're starting to use screens rather than, you know, print outs that go "blublublu" with little dots down the edges, right. So that was starting to happen. So.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: We knew this was coming and then, well, how do you go and do a really good system for this? How do you make it work? And so there's steps along the way, had conversations, if I want to name drop a little bit, with Stephen Wolfram and with Richard Feynman... And we talked about how much information is there? And so it's not sort of out the OK, if you had the... Encyclopedia Britannica, had a little index that had a micropedia then a macropedia and how many more steps before you get everything in the Library of Congress? And it just turned out to not be that big! But, you know, this was a time when we were building a supercomputer that had 32 MB of RAM, really. And we were building the biggest disk system. It was the size of a of a of a bar. Right? Of a drinking bar. That was the first RAID system. And it had five gigabytes in it, right? So this is the the high end, multimillion dollar supercomputer of the mid 1980s. But we knew that it was going on a particular curve. So we just stood out the curve and said, all right, when will this be doable? And it was, you know, decade, a couple of decades. But it was, you know, three decades. And we would be all the technology would be there!

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: And this is at Thinking Machines, then?

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: So this is this is all I left MIT to help build a supercomputer and then use that supercomputer to help do searching... of data, because I figured you wanted to it. We were trying to build smart machines, thinking machines. Danny's motto was, we want to build a machine that's proud of us. All right. And how do you how do you bring up the next generation, right? If humans are one generation and computers are the next, how do you bring up... You want to make the computers interesting to talk to and teach and then they want you want them to be useful to you so that there's ongoing back and forth. So we needed to all be done with human language. So we needed to be able to ask the computer questions in English, in natural language. And it wasn't voice at that point. We didn't know how to do that, but we could type. And so it wasn't, you know, these queries. It was... So we did the first sort of free form text database and Dow Jones bought it. And that's where I met Bill Dunn.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: OK. And so this is the WAIS system that you start at Thinking Machines, and then it gets spun off as a separate company, right?

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Yes. Starts at Thinking Machines and we work with... What we did, the search system. And then Dow Jones bought it. And then I found that the world didn't turn, you know, didn't... The sun didn't come up with different color. I mean, it was like, OK, what are we missing? And I said, we need personal, corporate and wide area information all woven into the same system. We needed to be able to be asked for by expensive people without delegating. Right? It wasn't a "call your librarian or your assistant to do it for you." It was, you know, we wanted... So we did a system that we prototyped with KPMG Pete Marwick. So 100 $400 dollars an hour people, Dow Jones for the wide area information, we indexed all of their corporate stuff that we could and made it so you could search your own personal email. All in the same system, so you can ask your email, your corporate in the wide information, all in one smooth system. It was called WAIS, wide area information servers. So that was a joint project with Dow Jones, Thinking Machines, KPMG Pete Marwick and Apple Computer.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: OK

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And that was started in 1989. And I spun that off as a company in 1992, but in 1991 we made a freeware release and that's what started going viral on this new thing called the Internet. And so it came out... my claim to fame there was that it came out before the web, you know. Yeah. Web was being used internally and since 1989, but hadn't sort of rolled out and it was sort of in the era of Gopher. And so there are a bunch of these systems and they all kind of rolled into the hypertext of the web, the search of WAIS, the multi-stop thing of Gopher all got rolled up into Mosaic and the web was the front end to all of these other systems. And so that happened sort of the early 90s, but the key thing for me was to get publishers on board. So we got Dow Jones, New York Times. Encyclopedia Britannica, Scholastic, CMP a tech Publisher, we got all these publishers to invest in this open Internet thing, which was really early to try to anchor an open world as opposed to the closed world of AOL or Lexis|Nexis.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And I needed open protocols to work so WAIS had Z39.50 at the core of it. There is a web, [which] was a much simpler HTTP system. And... we started doing well because we really needed to get this open world, what we didn't get at that time was [a] business model beyond advertising. We did the first advertising based websites at WAIS Incorporated. To just try to anchor the Open Web. So one of the cool things was that AOL had a business model where they shared revenue. So they made six dollars an hour and about 10 or 15 percent of that went to publishers that kept you online. So they had a royalty model. And I like royalties... you know how books work. And I would prefer it to advertising based systems. But at the time I sold WAIS to AOL, which was to try to get all that to work, to get them to scale that business model. They changed their business model to where they actually charge publishers to get to their eyeballs. And that was, so that's fundamentally an advertising-based gimmick. And so that didn't work very well for me, for AOL. I mean, and it's still not working very well for the Internet business model. It's plagued with problems, which is why we're seeing democracy undermined based on advertising business.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah, and I know...

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: So Fox News, you know, all all these sorts of problems. Right? And we know about those. So we have some work to do.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah. No. And it's been there for a long time. So we're at Thinking Machines to WAIS to then AOL. And I've sort of seen in magazine interviews and things I've been reading about... The first time I've seen mentioned this. And I'm curious what you think is was while, you're at AOL, I start to see mention of something called the "Library of Alexandria Foundation," just just sort of once or twice I've seen in some of the media. And so maybe you could speak a bit on that, on that. And how does this Library of Alexandria idea might have been percolating around at this time?

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Sure. I mean, you know, once you have publishing going, actually, let's take it back to Richard Feynman and then the conversations then? We just said, why don't we just buy a library and just, you know, cut off the bindings and poof - digitize? Right. And and the other thing, we could do that... but it doesn't have an ongoing system working. So I invested in trying to get the publishing system online and to get a business model for them so, you know, those guys would do their their thing, then we could build the library. So once we could get the publishers on board, then the whole idea was to try to go and build the library.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And so when I left AOL in 1995, I said, "OK, you know, now we have publishing going well enough." We didn't have the business models worked out, because we screwed up on that, but we did have... we got a critical mass of publishers' when... Microsoft in 1995 was working on a thing called "Blackbird," which was a competitor to AOL, and they changed direction and they swivelled their turret... their cannon towards Netscape and in the summer of 1995. And when that happened, it was like, "OK, good, the web, you know, if you have the most monopolistic, powerful tech company trying to kill the World Wide Web. The World Wide Web has made it!" [Laughs] So and so. That.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: I thought I could then move to doing the library, so that... we formed Alexa Internet. Short for the Library of Alexandria. And the Internet Archive on the same day in April of 1996 and wrote a contract into the soul of Alexa Internet: it would donate everything, all the data collected to the Internet Archive. And the names are a little different exactly then, it's shifted around a little bit, but but but that structure is basically what happened.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And interestingly for starting in 1996, through the end of 2020, Alexa Internet every day donated data to the Internet Archive.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And the only reason why it doesn't have to anymore is the Internet Archive is kind of up and running on its own, and it's using the data that the Internet Archive is helping build! So it's so it made it through the start-up phase and the acquisition and Interesting conversation with Jeff Bezos. And high integrity on the part of Amazon, because Alexa Internet didn't have a business model that worked. I mean, it had a toolbar that basically helped try to understand where people were moving around on the net to go and help people who like this website, like that website. And we were the first at scale [for] what became called collaborative filtering. And it's famous by the people who bought this one, bought that one. Right. So Amazon used that idea that technology... it was really, that idea came from Karl Feynman, son of Richard Feynman.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And and then he did it as his PhD or master's project. And then Firefly by Patti Moss, spun off out of MIT, was sort of the first of the of the real commercial uses of collaborative filtering. For me, I was going back to Bill Dunn, who said the metadata is more important than the data itself. So you're going to learn more about the Web by looking at how it's used than you are by reading the Web pages.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And I needed a... We needed the World Wide Web to win. And I thought that the search engines were only going to get so good that they were going to have real troubles unless they had a lot of usage information. And I was right... but wrong that it wasn't going to be done based on a toolbar, it was going to be based on how Google did it, which was looking at PageRank and anchor text. And they also track what people clicked. So they had a lot of visibility and that's how they made a Web search system that worked so well. It wasn't what AltaVista did with Inktomi, which was to fundamentally use the terms on the Web pages to answer your questions.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: It was a part of it for Google, but it's a small part [laughs] of the ranking.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah. So it's April 1996, the Internet Archive, Alexa Internet are formed. One thing I found neat is I've be looking at other Web archives and, you know, the first sort of web archiving event I'd sort of see in the United States is at the Smithsonian in March 1996. Where you're there, you're there in spirit at the Smithsonian. You launched this election 1996 archive. And I find that is... do you remember that at all? That was done in partnership with Internet Archive before it was formed, I think?

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah was it March? Interesting. So yeah. Maybe we hadn't incorporated yet. So I wanted to crawl the World Wide Web and all... My lawyer friend just said, you know, "they're going to kill you right there. You know, you can't you know, they're not going to let you live. They will they will run you down, strangle you and, you know, bury you in a shallow grave. Their lawyers are going to rain on you like frogs."

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And so I said no, "but it's a library!" And so we went to my friends at the Library of Congress because I've been working with them since early 90s and they weren't ready for it. They they... But the Smithsonian! And it was really it's always a person. Right. So it's David Allison at the Smithsonian, he was in charge of the American Museum, the Smithsonian Museum of American History. And they had a room of presidential memorabilia. And he said, you know, this Internet might become something. So the first websites might be like the first bumper stickers! And so, to his credit, to you know, basically I was still working, you know, in my house, right in an attic with, you know, a little tape robot, you know, in the garage. Right.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And and we proposed with them to go and archive this 1996 presidential election Web sites and because I'd worked on the 1992 presidential election... But anyway, so but and they said "great!" And they gave us a piece of paper with the with the with the sunburst [logo] on it saying, yes, we're doing it with them.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And they knew exactly why we needed that piece of paper!

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And and they did it... And they we did this project, we handed it off and they put a computer on the table next to the first bumper stickers, you know, in Rutherford B. Hayes's buttons, you know, and anyway. And that was a display. And the Smithsonian.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Ok. Yeah, I have seen that... I've seen the templated letterhead that went out to various parties saying we're going to archive your website, here's some details about it. So that's that's great.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: So we we archive these things. And by 2000, the Library of Congress was ready. But this was still before the Wayback Machine existed.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. I'll come back, because - cool - I've read some interesting stuff about that and the Library of Congress. But before we get to that, I might... Could you speak just a little bit about that process of setting up the Internet Archive and Alexa Internet? The infrastructure, the location, the early employees, like how how you build these two companies at the same time? I mean, you had money, but I don't imagine it was limitless amounts of money to do such an ambitious thing?

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Oh, no, no, no, no. But I had some money because we'd sold the company to AOL and I didn't know how to run a nonprofit. I knew how to do a for-profit. So I knew how to sell things to people. But I didn't know how to beg for money. And I still don't know how to beg for money. It's really not good at that. So really, Alexa Internet was the thing that employed people. And so we did it as a company. If there's one thing you know about companies, is they're not going to last, right? Companies self-destruct or they get acquired or they just, you know, they flub it. Right. Just so you know, companies are, I think... Of money and for profit companies like gasoline and just, you know, fire and it just goes WHOOSH. It is like and that's that!

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: But if you want something that lasts, build a non-profit, which is I really learned from my wife who is working and doing museums, and she was a print historian. And so a lot of my wife weaves all the way through, of course, my story and so we incorporate both of these at the same time, but the people worked for the for- profit. And and we got a little bit of investment from me and then Bill Dunn and then Danny Hillis helped arrange a significant investment. As a for profit startup.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And the idea was to build, to collect the web and then go in and help people navigate the Web by this collaborative filtering that would show you information about the website you're looking at. Cataloging the web, fundamentally it's cataloging the web. It was the Library of Alexandria. It was about going and saying, where are you and where do you want to go next? And it was a toolbar that just automatically updated, giving you information about where you are. And it would go and say, you know, are you in the way out back or are you like in some place central? Have people go in and commented that this place that this article is his hoo-hah? Right. It's all in context and all of that information that librarians understand and I understood by being a library tradition. I never got my full degree, but I did that. I guess I should go back to that in the 80s.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: But anyway, so what? We wanted to build a catalog of the Web and help people navigate it so that it would be there for people past the search engines and try to help you kind of know are you being lied to (which wouldn't it be great if that were more easy now?). But anyway, there's just some things to accomplish that that I think were good ideas. [pause] OK, so, um, yeah, so we we had a little bit of startup money. Oh and we put it in the Presidio of San Francisco! So this was "the impossible to do." I learned this from Thinking Machines that you should work in someplace interesting and beautiful. Because if you're working in Suite 201 in some anonymous office park, you will start thinking like Suite 201 in some anonymous office park, you will just start thinking generically. Thinking Machines was in a Victorian mansion in the middle of the woods. So we would go and it's just fabulous. And when I was in college, I was in Richardson Mansion, which is top architects, beautiful mansion in Boston. And so when we started WAIS, we started in a mansion in Menlo Park, not in an office [park].

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And when we started the Internet Archive, we were the second... we started in the Presidio by basically using a conference room at the Tides Foundation. And then from there we got our own little building where the second leaseholder in this new national park that had just been converted from being an office right in the center of San Francisco. It's completely beautiful.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: So that that gave us a home that was special and so people could really understand they're trying to do something, you know, big, right? The National Park, you know, they... you know, you don't get into the National Parks where you get to rent a place in a National Park and this is, you know, so, you know, the brim, the hat... Smokey the Bear was our landlord! And, you know, he said, well, you know, we want to we want to build the Library of Alexandria version two. We want to archive! We want to basically build a library of everything ever published.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And the guy's answer, Arnie Rossie, said, "well, you're either crazy or you're on to something. Either way, you're one of us."
segments.clip_title: Either Way, You're One of Us

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah, that's great.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And so that he said "welcome aboard." And so we rented a place there and that we got we rented more and more buildings in the Presidio. And so we kind of needed our own. And then we bought a former church!

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: And yeah, and sort of so Alexa hires the people, Alexa's the business. And, does the Internet Archive like own the tape machines? I've heard descriptions in the reading I've done like, these like jukeboxes in this Presidio office...

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Oh, you know, we've got the pictures so cool, right? Because disk drives were really expensive. You know, these are these are a time when you had a nine gigabyte hard drives that were, you know, super expensive.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And so the only way to really a cost effectively store gigabytes of data was on tapes. But if you had tapes, then they stack up and you can't access them. So there are these tape robots and [laughs] there were these miracle machines, right! They pull this tape out and go rrrrr, then you put it in and then go and then spin it up and three minutes later, they would seek the right place and you get your webpage back. It's like, wow! Really slow. But it did work. And we broke the tape machine just constantly. I mean, our joke was that the repair guy from Storage Tech, we should issue him an employee badge into our little house in the Presidio. I mean, this is a tiny little house, right? This is a couple of thousand square foot house in the prairie- house. And it had this tape robot in it that went rrrrr. But because we used it all the time, it just broke all the time.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: So eventually we try to by 1999, we moved to hard drives. And but hard drives were still really expensive, and so there's there's a problem, I apologize. Our images that we collected from around the year to 1999, 2000, 2001, where we're lower. We tried to make sure we could keep up with the HTML, but the images are largely missing from that era.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Well, that makes sense from my own use! I've wondered about that too, that's....

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Sorry.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: No, that's the transition! I'll come back to that shortly because I'm curious about that access transition as well. But so this is like 1996, 1997. And there's other... What I'm curious about is the role of national libraries, so you're setting this up in the Presidio... but then I'd be curious, because elsewhere around the world, we're seeing people kind of do the same thing as you. So Canada has a small pilot in '94. It doesn't really go anywhere. But then Australia and Sweden... in 1996 they start doing...

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: The Swedish guys visited us in our little house in the Presidio. And they were they were moving along, we really wanted to. I just wanted to work with the Library Congress, so I asked Winston Tabb, who's just fabulous, he was the Deputy Librarian of Congress. And I said when I was starting in 1996, I said, "Winston, why don't we just be the digital wing of the Library of Congress? You're not doing anything really ... [mumbles theatrically], so why don't we just be your digital wing?"

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And he said something to me that was just another one of those lines that has stuck with me forever. He said. "Brewster..." he's very diplomatic, "good idea, good idea. But don't do it too soon, it will only hold you back."

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: And it was so what that turned into was a relationship where we could do things they couldn't do or they didn't feel that they could do, but they gave us kind of an umbrella.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: Right, and so they had plausible deniability, so if we got shot up then, you know, they wouldn't get dragged into the lawsuits or whatever, but we also kind of leverage their patina. And it was I wouldn't do things that they wouldn't that they said don't do. But I I could do things that were a step ahead of where they thought they could be. Like archiving the presidential election websites in 96, or we cooperated in 2000 where we couldn't... We did the website, the election websites of 2000 with their funding. Good. But then making a Wayback Machine was a step beyond where they thought I could go. And when we launched that in October, 24th of 2001, they knew of it. They were nervous.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: [Laughs] And we launched it at the Bancroft Library with Larry Lessig and the head of the journalism school and the head of the Bancroft Library. You know, the walls and the ancient things. I mean, the Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley is a beautiful environment, right? And Berkeley knew exactly what they were doing by going and giving this new upstart idea that kind of a venue for launching the Wayback Machine.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, so that's a great relationship with the LC was sort of even before the official stuff starts in 2000, that was percolating..

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: I started working with them in 1992.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: They funded work on the WAIS program. I was keen for me to keep the Library of Congress involved.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: And and you mentioned the Swedes, so like, did Sweden come up with their idea... because, they're the big starter National Library grabbing, you know, they try to grab all of their Swedish domain. Did they come up with that on their own? Had they been talking to you? Is this, are these sort of birds of a feather or was there some communication?

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: I don't know. You'll have to ask them.

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Brewster Kahle
segments.text: I mean, I think the first real pronouncement of this publicly was in an American, Scientific American article...

segments.speaker: Ian Milligan
